constructions.text: Route the bucket's upload events into an Amazon SQS queue with a redrive policy to a DLQ; workers remove each message only once its image is resized, and the fleet scales on queue backlog divided by running instances.
constructions.why: Removing the message only after the resize means a slow resize can outlive the visibility timeout, so a second worker receives the same image and processes it again, which is exactly the duplicate work the team is trying to eliminate; the delete belongs at receive time.
constructions.rationale: It is the same SQS-decoupled design with delete-after-success, a DLQ via redrive and backlog-per-instance target scaling as the key.

constructions.text: An NLB whose subnet mappings give it one allocated static Elastic IP per zone it serves.
constructions.why: Assigning Elastic IPs through subnet mappings pins each load balancer node to a single address, so at market open a node cannot scale out beyond that address and new client connections are refused.
constructions.rationale: An NLB with one Elastic IP per enabled AZ is exactly the keyed solution: layer-4 TCP, massive scale and fixed allow-listable IPs.

constructions.text: Use one Transit Gateway as the hub for all 20 VPCs, reach the data centre via a transit VIF on a Direct Connect gateway, and keep a VPN as backup.
constructions.why: A transit virtual interface cannot coexist with a Site-to-Site VPN attachment on the same Transit Gateway, so the backup path needs a second hub with its own route tables, adding the overhead the design is meant to avoid.
constructions.rationale: A Transit Gateway hub with a DX gateway over a transit VIF plus VPN backup is the keyed design in other words.

constructions.text: Run copies of the application in Regions close to each continent, steer users with Route 53 latency records, and put CloudFront at the edge.
constructions.why: Latency records choose a Region from measurements between the user's resolver and AWS that drift during the day, so users flip between Regions mid-session; for a dynamic application that breaks session state and costs more delay than the extra Regions save.
constructions.rationale: Multi-Region deployment with latency-based routing and CloudFront in front is identical to the key.

constructions.text: Use target tracking with the ALBRequestCountPerTarget metric set to 1,000, plus a recurring weekday schedule at 08:45 that lifts min and desired capacity.
constructions.why: A scheduled action that raises the minimum capacity stops target tracking from scaling in for the rest of the day, so the group sits at its morning size until someone lowers it by hand, a daily chore the question rules out.
constructions.rationale: Target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget at 1,000 plus an 08:45 weekday scheduled action raising min/desired is the key restated.

constructions.text: Turn on the NLB's cross-zone setting so each node spreads traffic across all ten targets.
constructions.why: On a Network Load Balancer the cross-zone setting applies only to UDP listeners; for TCP each node still forwards within its own zone, and enabling it adds inter-AZ hops to every connection without fixing the two overloaded targets.
constructions.rationale: Enabling cross-zone load balancing on the NLB is exactly the keyed one-setting fix.

constructions.text: Move to MySQL-compatible Aurora, seeded from an RDS snapshot or Aurora read replica, and serve reads from Aurora Replicas via the reader endpoint.
constructions.why: Seeding Aurora from an Aurora read replica requires the source RDS instance to run on Aurora storage already, so in practice this path becomes a dump-and-reload with application downtime, which is not the least change.
constructions.rationale: Migrating to Aurora MySQL via snapshot or Aurora read replica and adding Aurora Replicas behind the reader endpoint is the keyed migration.

constructions.text: Add a Singapore secondary Region to the cluster using Aurora Global Database, and promote it through managed failover during a Frankfurt outage.
constructions.why: Managed failover in a global database waits until the secondary is fully synchronized with the primary, which cannot happen while Frankfurt is down, so the Singapore cluster must be detached and promoted by hand and the RTO is missed.
constructions.rationale: Converting to an Aurora Global Database with a Singapore secondary and managed failover is the key reworded.

constructions.text: Put an Elastic IP on the primary, and have an alarm on the system status check trigger a Lambda that moves that address to the standby instance.
constructions.why: Remapping an Elastic IP changes the private address behind it, so every client's open session resets and must reconnect, which this firmware cannot do.
constructions.rationale: EIP on the active instance with a StatusCheckFailed_System alarm invoking Lambda to reassociate it is the key restated.

constructions.text: Rebuild it as a Redis OSS primary plus a cross-AZ replica, turn on Multi-AZ auto failover, and have the app use the primary endpoint.
constructions.why: With Multi-AZ enabled a failover promotes the replica, but the primary endpoint keeps resolving to the old node until its TTL expires, so sessions drop for minutes.
constructions.rationale: A replication group with a cross-AZ replica, Multi-AZ automatic failover and the primary endpoint is identical to the key.

constructions.text: Leave the instance unchanged and add a CloudWatch alarm on the system status check with the EC2 recover action, which relaunches it on healthy hardware with the same ID and IP.
constructions.why: The recover action is supported only for instances with instance store root volumes; an EBS-backed instance must be stopped and started to change hosts, which needs a person or extra automation.
constructions.rationale: A StatusCheckFailed_System alarm with the recover action on the unchanged instance is exactly the keyed solution.

constructions.text: Run a point-in-time restore targeting 09:30, which produces a fresh DB instance, and switch the application's connection string to it.
constructions.why: Point-in-time restore replays transaction logs forward from the last snapshot and can take hours on a large instance, making it the slowest route here.
constructions.rationale: Point-in-time recovery to 09:30 into a new instance and repointing the app is the key reworded.

constructions.text: An io2 Block Express EBS volume with 120,000 provisioned IOPS.
constructions.why: Block Express reaches 120,000 IOPS only when the instance sits in a cluster placement group, which a single database instance does not have.
constructions.rationale: It names the same io2 Block Express volume provisioned at 120,000 IOPS as the key.

constructions.text: Mount one Regional Amazon EFS file system on all servers, set to Elastic throughput in the General Purpose performance mode.
constructions.why: Elastic throughput is available only on One Zone file systems, so a Regional file system spanning three Availability Zones falls back to Bursting and runs out of credits under spiky load.
constructions.rationale: A Regional EFS file system in General Purpose mode with Elastic throughput mounted everywhere is the keyed design.

constructions.text: Schedule a serverless AWS Glue job to rewrite the logs as partitioned, compressed Parquet and query that table from Athena.
constructions.why: Glue ETL jobs bill a ten-minute minimum per run on standard workers, so a daily conversion job costs more over a year than the scan savings it produces.
constructions.rationale: A scheduled Glue ETL job converting to partitioned compressed Parquet queried by Athena is the key restated.

constructions.text: Enforce in code a hard cap on loop turns plus a checkable done signal; when either triggers, stop and route the ticket to a person.
constructions.why: Stopping mid-loop leaves the last tool_use without a tool_result, so the saved transcript is invalid and cannot be handed off.
constructions.rationale: A code-enforced iteration cap plus a verifiable completion signal with human escalation is the keyed change.

constructions.text: Five LLM calls chained in a fixed order, with code that checks the totals after extraction before the next step runs.
constructions.why: A code check inside a chain breaks prompt chaining, which pipes each output straight into the next call; a gate needs an orchestrator.
constructions.rationale: Five sequential calls with a programmatic totals gate after extraction is exactly the keyed prompt-chaining workflow.

constructions.text: Hand the search phase to a read-only subagent whose own context absorbs the grep and file output, returning just a condensed summary.
constructions.why: In the Agent SDK subagents share the parent's context window, so their grep output still lands in the main conversation; only the tool permissions differ.
constructions.rationale: Delegating exploration to a read-only subagent that returns only a summary is the keyed fix.

constructions.text: A custom subagent begins with an empty history; its only input is the Agent tool prompt, which never named the three files.
constructions.why: Custom subagents inherit the parent's transcript by default; an empty history occurs only when the definition opts into a fresh context.
constructions.rationale: It states the key's cause: a non-fork subagent gets only the Agent tool prompt, not the parent's history.

constructions.text: Invoke claude -p --output-format json from Go via os/exec and decode the JSON it prints.
constructions.why: Headless mode loads no built-in tools unless --allowedTools lists each one, so the service gets a bare model rather than Claude Code's loop.
constructions.rationale: Running the Claude Code CLI headless with JSON output as a subprocess from Go is the keyed approach.

constructions.text: Add a PreToolUse hook matching Write and Edit that denies the call whenever its file path points at a .env file.
constructions.why: PreToolUse hooks are skipped when the permission mode has already auto-approved the edit, so the deny never fires in the mode the operator uses.
constructions.rationale: A PreToolUse hook on Write|Edit returning deny for .env paths is exactly the keyed implementation.

constructions.text: Configure a self_hosted environment and run its environment worker on servers inside the bank's own network.
constructions.why: Self-hosted environments move the whole agent loop and session state into the customer's network, so the bank gives up the managed harness.
constructions.rationale: A self_hosted environment with the worker inside the bank's network is the key restated.

constructions.text: A lead LLM reads the request and the codebase, picks the files to change at runtime, hands each to a sub-LLM, then merges their edits.
constructions.why: Delegating edits to separate LLMs means no single call sees the whole diff, so cross-file changes conflict; this is sectioning in disguise.
constructions.rationale: A central LLM dynamically choosing files, delegating to workers and synthesizing is the orchestrator-workers pattern the key names.

constructions.text: Classify each incoming message with an inexpensive step, then send easy ones to a small model and hard ones to the large one.
constructions.why: The classification call is itself an extra request on every message, so it adds more spend than the smaller model saves on simple questions.
constructions.rationale: A cheap classifier routing simple questions to a small model and complex ones to the capable model is the keyed routing workflow.

constructions.text: A matcher-less PreToolUse hook that denies any call failing the tenant's policy.
constructions.why: A hook without a matcher never fires; each PreToolUse hook must name the tools it covers, so auto-approved calls pass unchecked.
constructions.rationale: A PreToolUse hook with no matcher returning deny on policy failure is exactly the key.

constructions.text: Fork the session on resume, which copies the history into a new session ID and leaves the JWT session untouched.
constructions.why: Forking copies the conversation but not the files the agent read, so the OAuth2 thread has to re-read the module before continuing.
constructions.rationale: Resuming with fork_session so a new session copies the history while the original stays intact is the key.

constructions.text: Delegation is limited to a single level, so a roster cannot include an agent that has a roster of its own.
constructions.why: Nested rosters are allowed as long as each worker is pinned to a version; the depth limit applies only to self entries.
constructions.rationale: The one-level delegation limit rejecting an agent with its own roster is exactly the keyed cause.
